title: Whose machine is it, anyway?
text: For decades the received wisdom {{1}} simple: gadgets belonged to their makers. The argument ran {{2}} opening the case was hacking, spare parts and manuals, {{3}} once reached every repair shop, became restricted, and glue replaced screws. Farmers, {{4}} tractors refuse to start {{5}} an authorised dealer signs off, were among the first to revolt, and campaigners {{6}} pushed for a legal right to repair followed. {{7}} was the clamour that regulators on both sides of the Atlantic now require spare parts, manuals and unlockable diagnostics for years after a product goes on sale. The deeper question the movement raises is philosophical {{8}} practical: if you bought it, whose object is it — the maker's or yours?
